Nov. 26, 2018: Mars InSight lander touches down

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (386 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that inSight, short for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy, and Heat Transport, landed on Mars Nov.
  • Recent findings suggest that in addition to bountiful seismic data, which included more than 1,300 marsquakes, InSight recorded about a year’s worth of weather data at the lander’s location with unprecedented accuracy, according to Bruce Banerdt, the mission’s principal investigator and principal research scientist.
  • Not everything was a rousing success, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that inSight, short for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy, and Heat Transport, landed on Mars Nov. 26, 2018, tasked with a simple yet challenging mission: unlock the mysteries of Mars’ interior. Top priorities included uncovering Mars’ internal structure by measuring the thickness of the crust, obtaining the size and density of the core, and sussing out the structure and composition of Mars’ mantle.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to bountiful seismic data, which included more than 1,300 marsquakes, InSight recorded about a year’s worth of weather data at the lander’s location with unprecedented accuracy, according to Bruce Banerdt, the mission’s principal investigator and principal research scientist. The InSight lander also took the first magnetic field measurements on the surface of Mars and measured several properties of the soil around it.

Not everything was a rousing success, however. Most famously, the mission’s “mole” subsurface probe only penetrated about 16 inches (40 centimeters) deep, despite being designed to burrow to a depth of at least 3 feet (10 meters). It turned out that the soil beneath InSight’s struts was unlike any previously encountered on the surface; it simply didn’t cooperate with the instrument’s design. But even that cloud has a silver lining, as it provided scientists with important details about the terrain upon which InSight landed.

In a recent development, inSight’s successful initial two-year mission was extended to run at least through the end of December 2022. But the stationary lander relied on power generated from its two large solar panels, which steadily gathered dust. That dust reduced the panels’ efficiency over time, forcing mission planners to make tough choices regarding power allotment. In May of 2022, engineers placed the craft’s robotic arm into a final resting pose and turned off all its instruments, save one: InSight’s seismometer continued to operate on what little power was available, running about half the time, according to Banerdt. InSight last contacted Earth Dec. 15, 2022, after which two attempts were made to raise the lander. Both failed, and a few days later, NASA officially brought the mission to a close.

#145964. The closest exoplanets may host magnetic fields

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1420 w)

The closest exoplanets may host magnetic fields

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1420 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in all the universe, Earth is the only planet known to have life.
  • Recent findings suggest that but Earth is far from the only planet we know of.
  • Because of their protective role, magnetic fields have major implications in the search for life beyond Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in all the universe, Earth is the only planet known to have life. A big part of the reason life is possible here is our planet’s magnetic field. It acts like a shield, deflecting harmful energy from our Sun as well as cosmic rays from deep space that could otherwise erode Earth’s atmosphere and irradiate the surface, a death sentence for evolving life-forms.

Recent findings suggest that but Earth is far from the only planet we know of. As of this writing, there are more than 6,300 confirmed exoplanets on the roster, with more added by the day. Scientists have discovered stars with as many planets as our own Sun hosts. In other systems, planets as big as Jupiter whip around their sun in only a few days’ time. Astronomers have even discovered planets that orbit multiple stars at once, and they recently caught a glimpse of a possible atmosphere around a rocky, Earth-sized world in its star’s habitable zone. But until 2026, they had no compelling evidence that any terrestrial exoplanets had magnetic fields of their own.

Because of their protective role, magnetic fields have major implications in the search for life beyond Earth. Astronomers have long suspected that part of the reason Mars now appears dead is that its magnetic field fizzled out billions of years ago. This let the solar wind strip the water and other volatile compounds from its atmosphere, leaving it cold and barren.

Beyond the solar system, in 2019 researchers reported “indirect detections of exoplanetary magnetic fields” in four hot Jupiters. Then, a 2021 study found a strong signature of a magnetic field around HAT-P-11 b, a Neptune-like planet. Two years later, a pair of studies detected possible signs of a magnetic field around YZ Ceti b — this time, a rocky, Earth-like planet roughly the same size as, and only a bit less massive than our own. But this find has not yet been confirmed.

Industry observers note that in July 2026, a study published in Astronomy & Astrophysics found possible evidence of magnetic fields around two rocky exoplanets. Not just any exoplanets, either — Proxima Centauri b and d, the closest confirmed planets beyond our solar system, orbiting the red dwarf Proxima Centauri 4.2 light-years away.

Proxima b, roughly Earth’s mass and size, orbits every 11.1 days. Proxima d, likely a quarter to a third of our planet’s mass and 70% its size, orbits closer in with a period of 5.1 days. Because Proxima Centauri is smaller and less massive than our Sun, Proxima b is inside the habitable zone, where temperatures allow liquid surface water. A third planet, Proxima c, was tentatively detected in 2019 but is still unconfirmed. Astronomers don’t yet know if any of these worlds host atmospheres.

In a recent development, the fresh study, led by María Rosa Zapatero Osorio of the Centro de Astrobiología in Madrid, Spain, used 117 separate observations made with the Echelle SPectrograph for Rocky Exoplanets and Stable Spectroscopic Observations (ESPRESSO) instrument on the Very Large Telescope atop Cerro Paranal in Chile. The research followed up on previous studies conducted with ESPRESSO in 2020 and 2022, which focused on confirming the presence of planets around Proxima Centauri. Zapatero Osorio and her collaborators used the data to identify a peculiar correlation between the timing of flares emitted from Proxima Centauri and the orbital periods of its planets.

Sources indicate that “We detected low-energy flares occurring with a characteristic period of about 5.1 days,” Zapatero Osorio indicates. “This is very close to Proxima d’s orbital period.” But flares did not occur during every orbit of Proxima d, so the team ran statistical analyses to determine whether the flares were preferentially occurring at particular phases of the planet’s orbit. They found strong statistical evidence “that the occurrence of the flares is not randomly distributed over the planet’s orbital period,” Zapatero Osorio says. “Instead, a significant number of flares tend to occur at particular times in Proxima d’s orbit.” This is a possible indication that Proxima d could be interacting magnetically with its parent star, which would be likely to happen if the planet has a strong magnetic field of its own.

Recent findings suggest that using a model adapted from the physics of solar flares, Zapatero Osorio’s team calculated that Proxima d could have a magnetic field anywhere from 8 to 230 gauss in strength, with the best median estimate limited to around 16 gauss. This is about 27 times more powerful than Earth’s magnetic field (0.6 gauss), which protects life on Earth from the worst of the Sun’s energy.

According to recent reports, their model assumes that the star and planet are magnetically connected, Zapatero Osorio notes. Each sustains its own magnetic field, and these fields are interconnected. As a result of this connection, stress builds up on the stellar surface. From time to time, this stress is released in the form of low-energy flares, whose period is closely tied to the planet’s orbital period.

According to recent reports, although there was not as strong a correlation between Proxima b’s orbital period and the stellar flares, the team did find that Proxima b could also be interacting with the star, albeit in a lesser capacity. This suggests that although the finding is less sure, Proxima b may also sustain a magnetic field.

According to recent reports, there are alternative explanations for the findings. One possibility is that there could be intrinsic, long-lived active regions on Proxima Centauri itself that account for the peculiar timing of the flares. Another explanation is that gravitational interactions between the planets and Proxima Centauri could induce disturbances on the star without requiring a strong planetary magnetosphere, although the team suggests this is less likely. It’s also possible that when Proxima’s stellar wind reaches the planets, it interacts with them in a way that mimics the effects of a planetary magnetic field without requiring one.

In a recent development, like most red dwarfs, Proxima is a highly active star, regularly belching out intense flares that would be hazardous to any fledgling life-forms on the worlds in close orbit. Because Proxima is so close to Earth and has at least one rocky planet in its habitable zone, it makes a perfect testbed for studying how stellar flares could affect habitability around red dwarfs — the most common stars in the universe.

It has been revealed that astronomers looking for habitable worlds around these stars must contend with the likelihood that any planets would be effectively sterilized by the intense radiation in the flares constantly washing over them. Now, though, there is a glimmer of hope. If Proxima b and d do have magnetic fields, as this research suggests, they could act much like Earth’s own protective magnetic shield, deflecting enough harmful stellar radiation that life might just be able to take hold.

Sources indicate that “Earth’s magnetic field plays an important role in protecting life and supporting human progress,” says Zapatero Osorio. “It shields our planet from the solar wind and energetic particles, and it has also played an important role in navigation.”.

Unfortunately, Proxima d is so close to its host star that it is likely too hot to sustain life as we know it. Proxima b, however, lies within the habitable zone. “Based on the results of our study, both Proxima d and b may have magnetospheres capable of providing some protection against their host star’s activity,” Zapatero Osorio says.

Recent findings suggest that the importance of this find goes deeper than simply a pair of neighboring planets. In the last few years, evidence has emerged that gas giant exoplanets similar to Jupiter and Saturn host magnetic fields. These are the easiest types of planets to detect and study, but while magnetic fields around such worlds are certainly fascinating, the implications for planetary habitability are limited.

But as the number of known planets continues to swell, so, too, does our sample of Earth-like worlds. And if the two closest rocky planets beyond our solar system do indeed have magnetic fields, then perhaps these features are common. If true, it increases the chances that rocky worlds across the galaxy could be habitable — at least, for life-forms as we understand them. And the more planets capable of hosting life, the more likely it is that we might someday discover we are not alone.

Nick Oakes is a science writer for NASA’s Heliophysics Education Activation Team at Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.

Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug.
  • Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.
  • A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any fresh bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

According to recent reports, the House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances.

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., mentioned in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

It has been revealed that “Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”.

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At matter in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura noted his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change.

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He noted that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”.

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”.

Ors noted he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely newly introduced bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A upcoming Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

Latest Update: This man sometimes sees his cat’s eyes on people’s faces

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Industry observers note that after returning home from a 2024 brain surgery, a man started noticing something strange: Eyes that he had previously seen started showing up on the face he was right now looking at.
  • It has been revealed that “Right when I got home from the hospitals, I was seeing my cat in my mother and my sister,” says the 29-year-old teacher, who has asked to go by Karl to protect his privacy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that after returning home from a 2024 brain surgery, a man started noticing something strange: Eyes that he had previously seen started showing up on the face he was right now looking at. To his bewilderment, the swapping of features even extended to his pet cat Luna.

It has been revealed that “Right when I got home from the hospitals, I was seeing my cat in my mother and my sister,” says the 29-year-old teacher, who has asked to go by Karl to protect his privacy. “That was one of the first things that I noticed,” he says. “And the cat even took on resemblances of people.”.

It was unsettling, to say the least. “Looking at her and then looking at somebody else, I might see her giant eyes on a person.”.

Scientists have now described Karl’s perception of faces in the December issue of Cortex. His condition, in which echoes of a previously viewed image appear in a new context, is called palinopsia, and it was likely caused by Karl’s brain surgery. Because the echoes appear on faces, they distort how faces look to him, a condition known as prosopometamorphopsia. The new work offers clues about how brains perceive faces, both under normal and unusual conditions.

According to recent reports, the researchers’ analyses of the man’s face perceptions are “wonderfully innovative,” says clinical psychiatrist Jan Dirk Blom of Leiden University and Parnassia Psychiatric Institute in the Netherlands, who was not involved in the work. “In this era of big data and complex statistical analyses, we almost forget how informative clinical observations in single patients can be.”.

Karl’s unusual perceptions caught the attention of researchers. “His face processing system is disrupted, and it’s disrupted in a specific way,” says Brad Duchaine, a visual neuroscientist at Dartmouth University. “For reasons we don’t understand, items from memory are being pulled up and pasted onto the face that he’s perceiving.”.

Industry observers note that duchaine’s lab has been collecting case studies of people who perceive faces differently in an effort to learn about visual perception. Duchaine and his colleagues assessed Karl’s experiences by showing him images of faces and asking him to describe what he saw. This confirmed that he consistently saw distortions in the eye regions of faces, such as the shape, and in faces’ shading and sometimes even texture. As they worked together, Duchaine and Karl used AI-image generators to create pictures of faces that resemble what Karl saw for the cat-human swap.

In a recent development, karl isn’t the only person with palinopsia that affects faces, Duchaine says. A few other people have contacted him who also see echoes of prior faces. But Karl’s palinopsia seems different. “His were really consistent, very long-lasting. And then the cross-species transfer is something that I’d never heard before,” with one major exception, Duchaine says. A case study from 1986 describes a woman who, after seeing a poodle on a bus, saw poodle heads on every other passenger, too. That woman’s distortions lasted only about half an hour; Karl’s perceptual shifts have been consistently present since his 2024 surgery.

“What is new about the present study is the finding that a cat’s eyes can apparently be transposed from memory banks onto human faces observed in the here and now, and vice versa,” says Blom. “And that we now have a rough idea of the brain areas making this possible.”.

Industry observers note that during a surgery to correct malformed blood vessels, doctors removed tissue from Karl’s right posterior temporal area, a part of the brain known to be involved in face recognition. Karl’s experiences hint at how the visual system detects and interprets features on faces, Duchaine states. There’s an idea that humans interpret faces holistically, as a single object, he says. Karl’s case reveals some of the limits of this idea, because he’s having these effects specific to the eye region, Duchaine says.

“It’s sort of like a filter,” Karl indicates, describing his experience of palinopsia. “It decides on a style, and then that style is applied to everyone in my reality, including myself.” These filters can change across a day or last several weeks, Karl says. He’s even experienced eye feature swaps from a face he saw in a dream. “And that was then applied to me, looking in a mirror, and then everybody else.”Karl also experiences echoes of environments, he says. For instance, if he has visited an area with lots of potholes in the roads, visual echoes of those potholes can appear in a newer road. A similar thing can happen with shapes, he says: Echoes of square hallways or stairwells can appear in newly introduced spots.

Using AI and collaboration to help re-create what Karl sees is an advance, Blom states. And this sort of collaboration between scientist and volunteer is crucial. “In my line of work, clinical psychiatry, we know that everything stands and falls with the descriptions that our patients give us,” he says. “In my opinion, this is patient participation at its best.”.

The Sky This Week from November 27 to December 4: Brilliant Venus

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2025 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Friday, November 27As fall deepens and winter approaches, the wintertime star patterns are reappearing in our evening sky.
  • In a recent development, look east late tonight to locate the waning gibbous Moon near the border of Gemini and Cancer.
  • In a recent development, sunrise: 6:59 A.M.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Friday, November 27As fall deepens and winter approaches, the wintertime star patterns are reappearing in our evening sky. One is a large asterism called the Winter Hexagon, now fully above the horizon by about 10 P.M. local time. You should be able to spot this shape even with the Moon nearby, as each point in the Winter Hexagon is a bright, well-known star.

In a recent development, look east late tonight to locate the waning gibbous Moon near the border of Gemini and Cancer. This will help you find the first point in the Hexagon, the pair of stars Castor and Pollux, the heads of Gemini the Twins, glowing just above the Moon at this time. From there, look upward for another bright star in neighboring Auriga — this is Capella, the next point in the Hexagon. From Capella, look left and down just a little to find the V-shaped face of Taurus the Bull, where the bright star Aldebaran shines, marking the next point. Then it’s down to Orion’s bright knee, Rigel, before you drop down and a little left, close to the horizon, to land on Sirius, the brightest star in the sky and the nose of Canis Major. The Hexagon closes out with the luminary of the Little Dog, Procyon.

In a recent development, sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Recent findings suggest that saturday, November 28Saturn remains a bright naked-eye object all evening, setting around 2 A.M. local time. Around 8 P.M., you’ll find it high in the south, to the left of the Circlet of Pisces and above the body of Cetus the Whale.

It has been revealed that tonight and for the next few nights, Saturn’s strange, two-faced moon Iapetus is skimming north of the planet, making it easier to find. Now glowing at 11th magnitude, it is heading west toward a late December western elongation, when it will shine about a magnitude brighter but sit far from Saturn. Once you’ve got Saturn in your scope, look about 2’ northeast to land on Iapetus. Over the next few nights, it will move westward, reaching inferior conjunction and standing due north of the ringed world by the 30th.

According to recent reports, if you can catch 11th-magnitude Iapetus, you’ll also see four brighter moons: 10th-magnitude Dione, Rhea, and Tethys closer to Saturn; and mid-8th-magnitude Titan, about 3’ to Saturn’s west. The latter is the planet’s largest and brightest moon, easy to spot in any size scope and often even binoculars. If you keep returning each night to track Iapetus, also keep an eye on Titan, which is moving eastward toward the planet and will pass south of Saturn on December 2. Dione, Rhea, and Tethys have smaller orbits and shorter periods, so they move visibly over the course of several hours, frequently swapping places and passing in front of or behind Saturn. For example, Dione disappears behind Saturn’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 12:20 A.M. EST on the 29th (still late on the 28th in time zones farther west).

Sources indicate that sunrise: 7:00 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 9:10 P.M. Moonset: 11:09 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (73%).

Industry observers note that sunday, November 29Have you ever seen your shadow by planetlight? Venus reaches greatest brilliancy at 2 P.M. EST, now shining at magnitude –4.9. Rising nearly three and a half hours before the Sun, Venus will be so bright that it could potentially cast a shadow if you’re in a location with particularly dark skies (Bortle 1 or 2).

Even without perfect viewing conditions, this morning star can’t be missed. By an hour before sunrise, Venus is roughly 25° high in the southeast, blazing just to the lower left of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo. Far to Venus’ lower left, closer to the ground, Mercury stands nearly 5° above the horizon, shining at magnitude –0.7.

Recent findings suggest that compare the two planets through a telescope. Venus is a 27%-lit crescent, but its disk stretches 40” across. Mercury, by comparison, is much smaller, just 6” across, but its phase is 82%. Now through the first week of December is the best time to catch the solar system’s smallest planet, as it remains bright but appears to sink toward the horizon day by day. By the 5th, Mercury will be less than 2° high an hour before sunrise, making viewing challenging both because of potential obstacles on the horizon as well as the more turbulent layer of air near the ground.

Venus, meanwhile, stays at roughly the same altitude an hour before sunrise all month, its phase growing to nearly 50% lit by the end of the year. Earth’s sister planet will remain prominent in the morning sky through the first half of next year.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 7:01 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 10:25 P.M. Moonset: 11:43 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (62%).

It has been revealed that monday, November 30Venus remains a brilliant and unmissable morning star, but it’s not the only object worth paying attention to before dawn. Leo is hosting a celestial get-together this morning as the Moon joins two planets and the star that sits at the heart of the Lion, just beneath the Sickle asterism.

In a recent development, the waning gibbous Moon is the brightest object here; next brightest is Jupiter, located to the Moon’s upper right and glowing at magnitude –2.2. The gas giant stands nearly side by side with Mars (to Jupiter’s left); the Red Planet is fainter but still a respectable magnitude 0.4. Both planets are slowly growing in brightness and size as they approach opposition early next year. Through a telescope, Jupiter stretches 39” across, offering excellent views of its alternating light and dark cloud bands, and Mars is now 8” wide.

Shining between Mars and the Moon is 1st-magnitude Regulus, often drawn as both the heart of Leo and the base of the Sickle asterism’s handle. The curving backward question mark of stars that forms the Sickle’s blade and the Lion’s head in profile lies above the grouping in the sky before dawn.

Sliding along the ecliptic, the Moon passes 1.2° south of Jupiter at 4 A.M. EST, then 1.1° south of Regulus at 10 A.M. EST and 3° south of Mars at 3 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 7:02 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 11:36 P.M. Moonset: 12:11 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (51%).

Industry observers note that tuesday, December 1Last Quarter Moon occurs at 1:09 A.M. EST. A few hours later, asteroid 2 Pallas reaches a stationary point at 7 A.M. EST. Located in Cetus, it is visible all evening, setting around 1 A.M. local time. It stands highest around 8 P.M., when it’s roughly 30° above the southern horizon, about 4.2° southeast of 2nd-magnitude Diphda (Beta [β] Ceti).

According to recent reports, glowing at magnitude 9.0, Pallas is easy to find with a small scope. It sits near a neat triangle of 5th- to 6th-magnitude stars, which lie about 1.5° southwest of the asteroid and act as a great reference point to find it tonight. Pallas is 1° east of the easternmost star. Previously, Pallas was closing on that star, moving westward. But after tonight, it will turn and move slowly eastward again, pulling away from the little triangle night by night.

Industry observers note that drop about 5° south of this region for an added treat: 8th-magnitude globular cluster NGC 288, just over the celestial border in Sculptor. Spanning about 13’, this ancient ball of stars lies nearly 49,000 light-years away. It’s also near another deep-sky target, the 7th-magnitude galaxy NGC 253. Often called the Silver Coin or Sculptor Galaxy, this stunning edge-on spiral lies about 1.7° northwest of NGC 288 and can be viewed together with the cluster in wide-field instruments such as binoculars or finder scopes.

It has been revealed that sunrise: 7:03 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: — Moonset: 12:35 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (40%).

Recent findings suggest that wednesday, December 2It’s now asteroid 4 Vesta’s turn to reach a stationary point at 11 A.M. EST as it, too, swims through the domain of Cetus the Whale. Visible in the evening sky, Vesta sits more than 40° above the southern horizon around 7 P.M. local time. Previously moving retrograde, or westward, it will now begin moving prograde, or eastward, against the background stars.

Industry observers note that this month Vesta is located roughly halfway between bright Saturn to its northwest and magnitude 3.6 Theta (θ) Ceti to its southeast. Saturn is impossible to miss, as it’s the brightest object in this region of the sky. To locate 7th-magnitude Vesta, find Saturn early in the evening and slide about 8.1° east-southeast to land on the main-belt world. There aren’t a lot of background stars in the immediate vicinity, so try to match your view to the star chart above to locate the asteroid in your eyepiece. Because it’s moving slowly, you’ll need to come back every night or two to check out the view and note the light that’s shifted position — that’s Vesta.

It has been revealed that sunrise: 7:04 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 12:43 A.M. Moonset: 12:58 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (30%).

Thursday, December 3Look north a few hours after sunset to find the W-shaped star pattern of Cassiopeia on her head, looking more like the letter M as this circumpolar constellation swings above the North Celestial Pole. Just 1.9° northwest of Navi (Gamma [γ] Cassiopeiae), the midpoint of the M (or W), is a lovely open cluster cataloged as NGC 225 and known as the Sailboat Cluster.

Sources indicate that longtime Astronomy contributor Rod Pommier gave the cluster its nickname because he saw an arc of stars within the cluster that looked to him like the sail of a boat catching the wind, connected to a straight line of stars forming the mast and another eight stars outlining the vessel itself. The stars of the cluster are roughly 2,100 light-years distant, and this grouping was discovered by Caroline Herschel in 1783.

For added visual interest, the cluster is set against a complex of dark nebulae made of dust, which block the starlight behind them.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 7:05 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 1:49 A.M. Moonset: 1:20 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (21%).

Sources indicate that friday, December 4The waning Moon puts even faint deep-sky objects within reach on these early December evenings. Tonight, let’s look toward a distant elliptical galaxy nestled in the far southeastern corner of Lacerta the Lizard. Cataloged as NGC 7426, this 13th-magnitude stellar smudge sits close to a lovely pair of contrasting stars, making finding it a rewarding sight for all: While you do need a larger scope to track down the galaxy, the stars are visible even through smaller instruments, offering something for everyone.

It has been revealed that around 7 P.M. tonight, our target is still more than 35° high in the west. The zig-zagging figure of Lacerta sits just above cross-shaped Cygnus as the Summer Triangle sinks toward the western horizon. To Lacerta’s left (southeast) is Pegasus, and we’ll use 3rd-magnitude Matar (Eta [η] Pegasi) as our jumping-off point. From here, slide about 5° north-northeast to find a pair of stars, 6th and 8th magnitude, roughly 1’ apart. The brighter star glows blue-white, while its dimmer neighbor shines orangey-gold. NGC 7426 lies roughly 4’ east-northeast of this pair, appearing as a faint, grayish-white smudge. It measures roughly 2’ by 1.5’, its compact size helping to keep its faint light confined to a relatively small area.

Recent findings suggest that sunrise: 7:06 A.M. Sunset: 4:34 P.M. Moonrise: 2:54 A.M. Moonset: 1:44 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (14%).

Latest Update: Extinct, long-legged grasshoppers walked on water alongside dinosaurs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • In a recent development, nearly 100 million years ago, spindly legged grasshoppers may have scooted across water like modern day water striders.
  • Sources indicate that special hairs and leaf-shaped leg adornments, exquisitely preserved in amber, suggest the insects — members of a newfound family of insects — could balance and slide around on surface tension, researchers report November 24 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In a recent development, nearly 100 million years ago, spindly legged grasshoppers may have scooted across water like modern day water striders. The clues are in the fossilized insects’ legs and feet.

Sources indicate that special hairs and leaf-shaped leg adornments, exquisitely preserved in amber, suggest the insects — members of a newfound family of insects — could balance and slide around on surface tension, researchers report November 24 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The discovery suggests at least three insect groups evolved independently to move across water.

Paleontologist Chunpeng Xu and his colleagues first encountered the strange insects while studying a collection of 99-million-year-old amber. Frozen in time were three pieces of amber containing wingless grasshoppers with short bodies and incredibly long, skinny legs. Due to their unorthodox body shape, Xu didn’t recognize them as grasshoppers at first and thought they might be harvestmen or stick insects.“I was genuinely amazed,” says Xu, of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Paleontology in China. “They are among the most bizarre insects.”.

According to recent reports, under the microscope, two details stood out: Front legs with water repellant hairs and rear lower legs with leaf-shaped paddlelike structures. Estimates of the insects’ weight show they could have ridden on the water’s surface tension, with help from the repellant hairs on their legs and their spread-out footprint across the surface of the water. And the paddlelike lower legs would have propelled them forward.

The researchers named the insects Hydrelcana zhangi, placing them in the fresh family Hydrelcanidae.

“Walking on water is a pretty rare skill in nature,” Xu claims. Until now, only two insect groups were known to have evolved to live on the water’s surface: water striders and their kin, and a similar looking but unrelated, long extinct family called Chresmodidae.

The grasshoppers had a different gait from other water-walking insects. The common pond skater (Gerris lacustris), by comparison, rows with its middle limbs.

And whereas modern water-walking insects are predators and scavengers, the ancient grasshoppers were also probably herbivorous, given their mouthparts and lack of claws. The researchers found nine of them preserved in the same amber chunk, suggesting the insects may have gathered in large numbers to feed. It’s possibly the earliest record of such swarming behavior in grasshoppers or crickets, the team notes.

Solar lease holdouts still see value in privately-owned residential projects

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The One Major Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects.
  • Recent findings suggest that A residential solar project in Newly introduced York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions.
  • It has been revealed that after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The One Major Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects. The ITC is a historic renewable energy subsidy that provides a 30% tax credit against the total cost of an eligible project, and it is right now available to the commercial and utility-scale solar segments.

Recent findings suggest that A residential solar project in Newly introduced York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions. Credit: Nickels Energy Solutions.

It has been revealed that after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned. However, a loophole in the tax credit language has allowed leased or “third party-owned” (TPO) solar projects to still receive the ITC (25D) on residential solar projects. In this scenario, it matters who owns the solar project, not necessarily where it’s built. The project can be subsidized because it is owned by a commercial firm, and not the homeowner.

It has been revealed that some residential solar installers are still strictly pursuing and installing privately-owned solar projects. Nickels Energy Solutions (NES), a residential solar contractor working in Central Fresh York believes a privately-owned PV system is still the better deal for the customer.

It has been revealed that “We don’t have the same offers as some of the bigger companies,” stated Kevin Nickels, VP of sales with NES. “If you can offer leases, it’s like the ‘haves and have-nots.’ I don’t have that loophole or that trick up my sleeve, so it forces me to get the project sold, while I’m as sharp as I can be with margins to make it somewhat competitive.”.

TPO solar transactions are typically arranged at a lower up-front cost than a wholly owned solar project. Lease contract lengths vary by provider, and financiers have surety in these transactions because the projects will be built with products from an approved vendor list (AVL). Products on an AVL can qualify for a domestic content subsidy, another tax credit in addition to the ITC, because they are manufactured using a certain percentage of domestic components.

Sources indicate that these are premium products vetted for AVLs. But it can also mean that installers are paying premium prices for components in building TPO solar projects.

Nickels believes that, while a privately owned residential solar project will cost more at the start, the combination of expensive components and interest rates for financing over a lease term — with factors like rate increases — can cost a customer more in the long run.

“I don’t think all leases are bad,” he remarked. “I just don’t think it’s what’s best for the industry or the homeowner.”.

Selling residential solar in 2026.

Rudy Wright, owner of Wright-Way Solar of Tyler, Texas, has shifted the company’s focus from building upcoming projects to servicing existing systems. As the ITC exited the residential solar market, so did many of the lenders financing these projects. Without lending options, Wright-Way’s installation output has slowed down, and those clients who can afford solar are paying with cash or using a home equity loan to cover the cost.

Despite that, Wright remarked he isn’t very interested in building leased solar projects.

It has been revealed that wright-Way Solar built a solar plus storage project at a Ranch in Texas featuring arrays that are facing east, west and south. Credit: Wright-Way Solar.

Industry observers note that “I do think it cost me some of those entry level clients, but every time I analyzed the financing end of it, I felt like I was benefitting my manufacturer and the industry more than the customer,” Wright noted. “I haven’t seen the angle where bringing a pre-purchase agreement or bringing a lease agreement has enough ironclad return for the customer.”.

Tyler is a unique market for solar because many of Wright-Way’s customers are trying to make their properties more resilient, and less reliant on the grid, by installing solar and storage, and not just seeking cost savings for their energy use. Wright has installed solar plus storage systems on Texan ranches at a scale close a small commercial project.

That promise of resilience is still enough reason for some people to commission a solar project in Texas, where the state’s independent electrical grid operator has faltered and experienced dangerous outages in recent years.

“Folks realize money in the bank doesn’t do you any good if the power goes out,” Wright said.

NES is still building a steady pipeline of residential solar projects in Newly introduced York. Nickels said that has been possible in part because many of its clients are upper-middle class; but New York also maintains an incentive program for solar projects, NY-Sun, which includes a 25% state tax credit for residential systems.

“The OBBBA caught a lot of states flat-footed,” Nickels noted. “Without federal support, it puts a lot of pressure on what the state is offering.”.

In a recent development, some states’ solar subsidy programs have stepped in where federal support has diminished since the OBBBA was passed. The North Carolina Clean Energy Technology Center maintains the Database of State Incentives for Renewables & Efficiency, which analyzes which states currently have policies and incentives supporting clean energy developments. Every state has policy enabling solar projects, but not necessarily cost incentives for individual projects.

According to recent reports, while traditional residential solar projects have lost a significant subsidy, the reality is that energy costs have risen in response to newly introduced grid demands from hyperscale data centers and oil scarcity from the United States’ war in Iran. Sure, a privately owned residential solar project won’t receive the ITC, but it can still stabilize energy costs without them.

“We lost a major incentive, but the rate increase is proportional,” Nickels said.

Australia’s legless geckos evolved like snakes did

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (761 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • It has been revealed that australia’s limbless geckos look a lot like snakes.
  • Snakes are technically a highly modified group of legless lizards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that australia’s limbless geckos look a lot like snakes. It turns out they’ve evolved like snakes too.

Snakes are technically a highly modified group of legless lizards. Dozens of other lizard lineages have independently lost their legs, too. But the legless pygopod geckos aren’t quite like their slithering nonsnake kin. Pygopods have dietary pickiness and physical diversity patterns that are more reminiscent of those found in snakes than in other legless lizards, researchers report in a preprint posted at bioRxiv.org on October 23.

The 50 recognized species of pygopod geckos are found throughout Australia and Upcoming Guinea. Pygopods range from a meter long to the size of half a cooked spaghetti noodle. They have odd tails, which in some species can be fantastically long, exceeding 400 percent of their less-than-1-centimeter-long bodies. Some use their tails like a spring to leap.

“They create a little sine wave and they shoot themselves up in the air, and they can do successive jumps,” notes Ian Brennan, an evolutionary biologist at the Queensland Museum Kurilpa in Brisbane, Australia.

But not much else is known about them, Brennan claims.

Sources indicate that “They’re real oddballs,” he notes, noting that geckos are typically thought of as skilled climbers on walls or glass surfaces. “[Pygopods are] a group that’s gone the exact opposite direction.”.

As part of a large project tackling the genetics of Australia’s lizards and snakes, Brennan and his colleagues gathered data on pygopods’ genes, diet and physical features. They analyzed DNA from all 50 species of pygopod and generated an evolutionary tree. The team also put together data from the literature on the ratio of their body and tail lengths and compared this with a dataset of similar information on over 3,100 lizard and snake species.

As they evolved, snakes got longer by lengthening their bodies. Limbed lizards tend to get longer by lengthening their tails. The team found that pygopods have done both, an unusual strategy among legless lizards. This dual strategy resulted in some unexpected physical diversity in tail and body ratio.

Next, the team tackled diet, comparing between 1,738 lizard and snake species. Snakes as a group have a broad diet with lots of specialization, which might be partly why they’ve been so successful at diversifying into so many ecological roles in so many habitats, Brennan says. There are pythons that eat only large mammals and sea snakes that eat only fish eggs, for instance.

Industry observers note that this pattern is rare in lizards. Most geckos eat insects such as beetles and cockroaches, Brennan says. This is especially true of the legless groups, which mostly gobble down whatever insects they happen to slither past.

But the team found that the wide variety in what pygopods as a group will eat is exceeded among reptiles only by monitor lizards and colubrid snakes, a hyperdiverse group of over 2,000 snake species. Within that broad dietary range, particular pygopods flirt with snakelike pickiness. Some pygopods chiefly hunt spiders and scorpions. Another group targets ants and termites. One predatory pygopod — the Lialis genus — gulps down other lizards snake-style.

According to recent reports, pygopods’ evolutionary history may provide hints about how this heightened diversity developed. The team’s findings suggest they split off from other geckos in Australia 50 million years ago — much more recently than when the first snakes evolved around 160 million years ago, but before any modern snake groups reached Australia. Brennan thinks pygopods filled the roles of small snakes on the continent for millions of years in isolation.

According to recent reports, “Pygopods were probably on a trajectory to do something spectacular, like snakes,” notes Brennan. “But then all of these [snake] groups showed up in Australia and filled into those niches.”.

Sonal Singhal — an evolutionary biologist at California State University, Dominguez Hills in Carson — would like to see this study’s data combined with data on pygopods’ skull shape, their habitat use and how their bodies move.

“For example, Lialis can swallow prey whole because their jaws are so flexible and kinetic and their teeth hinge back and forth, allowing them to trap prey.”.

Sources indicate that for Brennan, a lesson from the findings is that lacking limbs need not be an evolutionary constraint. Both snakes and pygopods “have diversified to do really interesting things, either due to or in spite of being limbless,” he claims.

The 7 Best Garage Heaters for Your Workshop

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Garages and unfinished basements are often poorly insulated, making them prone to extreme cold in fall and winter.
  • Sources indicate that garage heaters come in various styles, though the most popular models are electric and propane.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Garages and unfinished basements are often poorly insulated, making them prone to extreme cold in fall and winter. A garage heater can turn this typically frigid space into a warm, practical area for woodworking projects, vehicle maintenance, and more. If you blueprint to spend time in your garage this winter tackling projects at your workbench, raising the ambient air temperature is a must.

Sources indicate that garage heaters come in various styles, though the most popular models are electric and propane. Electric heaters are convenient and easy to install if a power outlet is nearby. Propane heaters are more portable and can cover more surface area. Natural gas garage heaters are also powerful options for larger garages and can offer long-term heating solutions.

In a recent development, heaters can benefit not only comfort but also safety. Cold temps can cause condensation to collect on tools and stored items, which may lead to rust and other damage. Wintry environments can also cause car engines and batteries to wear out faster. A well-heated garage protects your investments and provides a warmer, safer place to work.

If you're ready to prep for winter weather, read on for our in-depth reviews of the best garage heaters, followed by the most vital things to know before buying.

Although we haven’t tested the models below ourselves, we applied our experience testing space heaters and patio heaters to supplement our search for the best garage heaters. We spent a lot of time vetting features and specs, checking manufacturer websites, gauging prices, and consulting user reviews before deciding which ones made the cut. We spoke with mechanical and electrical engineering experts to understand what makes a great garage heater, and we considered heat types (electric, propane, or kerosene), as well as whether the heaters are permanent or portable.

This 240-volt compact garage heater is the best all-around choice for most spaces, with 7,500 watts of heating power and the option to mount it on the wall or ceiling.

According to the manufacturer, it warms a typical garage or unheated building to between 50 and 85 degrees Fahrenheit and should be installed with a foot of clearance from combustible surfaces.

The garage heater’s adjustable louvers let you direct air where you need it most, and a remote-controlled thermostat is built into the front of the heater. A wall-mounted thermostat is available for the unit as well, but it’s sold separately.

Thanks to its Wi-Fi capability, you can operate this heater from virtually anywhere to ensure your garage is warm when you get home, or to heat the space before you spend time at your workbench. You can turn the unit on and off and set recurring schedules through the app.

The garage heater is rated to warm a 1,000-square-foot area, with an adjustable output of up to 20,000 BTUs. It can be mounted to the wall or ceiling, and its large digital temperature display is easy to read, even from across the room.

But for the price, it’s disappointing that the garage heater doesn’t include wiring.

For a powerful 5,600-watt portable garage heater, we recommend this NewAir model. It’s designed to warm spaces up to 600 square feet, and it includes a 6-foot cord that neatly coils on top of the unit, with brackets to hold it down.

The fan has two settings: automatic (which turns on when the heating element activates) and continuous. You can switch between the two manually.

Use continuous mode to keep air moving in spaces with high ceilings or when you’re operating an air-cleaning appliance, like a bench-top air filter, as it helps push dusty air through to speed up the process.

Sources indicate that designed for outdoor areas like patios, this Briza heater still works well in a garage thanks to its dust-resistant properties. It comes with an adjustable tripod that you can set between 44 and 84 inches tall. Selecting between its three heat settings—900, 1,200, or 1,500 watts—is easy with the unit’s remote control.

According to recent reports, the heater has a built-in safety sensor that automatically shuts the appliance off if it tips over. A timer provides additional safety (and energy savings) by automatically shutting the heater off after 1 to 9 hours of operation.

Recent findings suggest that for a compact, affordable garage heater ideal for targeted heating, this propane-fueled unit from Mr. Heater is a great choice. It delivers 4,000 to 9,000 BTUs from a single 1-pound liquid propane canister and can heat up to 250 square feet. It works great on the floor by your workbench or desk.

In a recent development, the heater can run for up to three hours on high, or you can upgrade to a 20-pound tank with a separately sold adapter. The heater’s size and weight make it easy to reposition, and it’s easy to bring with you to a shed, campsite, or other workspace.

This heavy-duty, 240-volt garage heater is ideal for climates with major temperature swings, featuring a two-stage high-and-low heating system.

Industry observers note that its lower heat output suits mildly cool days, while the higher stage can warm garages in single-digit temperatures. It also has a fan mode ideal for increasing airflow in a potentially stuffy garage, plus an energy-saving setting that defaults to the lowest wattage to maintain the desired temperature.

Industry observers note that A universal bracket is included for easy mounting to a ceiling or wall, and this heater has a remote-controlled thermostat. The only drawback is that it doesn’t offer much coverage for the price.

If you have an uninsulated wood garage or another minimally insulated space, this large, ceiling-mounted garage heater is worth a look.

Industry observers note that it runs on natural gas (a propane conversion kit is included) and, with a built-in electric fan, can warm areas up to 2,000 square feet thanks to its impressive 80,000-BTU output. It also has a powered exhaust that allows for vertical or horizontal venting.

Industry observers note that note that the Massive Maxx does not come ready to install; you’ll have to purchase a thermostat, gas hose, fittings, and regulator separately. For most people, it’s best to have a licensed heating-cooling contractor install this garage heater.

According to recent reports, there’s a lot to consider when using a heater to keep your garage safe and comfortable. So we picked the brain of Pat Porzio, a mechanical engineer and multi-licensed tradesman (electrical, plumbing, HVAC). He’s also the HVAC manager for Russo Brothers in East Hanover, New Jersey. We also spoke with David Shapiro, an electrician, author, and expert on old house wiring who contributes to electrical product and installation standards.

It has been revealed that both agree on one thing: Your overarching concern in heating a garage is safety. The first words out of both their mouths were identical: “Pull a permit.” That is, if you blueprint to use a permanently installed electric or gas-fired garage heater, you need to file a building permit for the work—whether you do the work yourself or hire a contractor. Permitted installations are inspected by the town or other authority with jurisdiction over this work where you live, which increases the likelihood of a safe installation.

Industry observers note that aside from pulling a building permit for the electrical work, Shapiro steers homeowners away from any heater without a UL (or other safety-related U.S. testing agency) listing.

Using a 120-volt space heater is simpler; same goes for small propane-fired and kerosene heaters. You don’t need a building permit to use one of these in a garage. Still, there are safe and unsafe ways to use these heaters. For more on that topic, check out our garage heater safety tips below.

Industry observers note that as we mentioned earlier, there are a couple of different types of garage heaters. Electric heaters are easier to install, don't require a vent, and are generally safer. But depending on your local electricity rates, they can be more expensive to run. Gas heaters use natural gas or propane, and they can be a more cost-effective option for heating larger garages. They require ventilation, which can be a pain if you don't already have the right setup.

It has been revealed that infrared heaters heat objects rather than the air, so they can be a good companion for localized projects at your workbench. Forced-air heaters use a fan to distribute heat quickly and work well for large spaces, but they require good insulation to run efficiently and may kick up dust around your workshop.

It has been revealed that for most garages, an electric heater is often the most viable option because it's easy to install, safe, and effective. But if you have a larger or poorly insulated garage, a gas heater might be the way to go.

In a recent development, “A bigger heater is not necessarily better,” Porzio claims. “An oversized heater will short cycle. That is, it will turn on and off too frequently. It satisfies heating demand very promptly and abruptly turns off. A heater that is too small will do just the opposite. It will run and run and never fulfill the heating demand, eventually wearing itself out.”.

According to recent reports, before contractors install a boiler or furnace, they perform a series of calculations, called a Manual J, to determine the correct size. While homeowners can get a rough estimate by multiplying the area's square footage by 50 to get the required BTUs, Porzio recommends using simplified Manual J forms online or a sizing tool like those on King-Electric.com and Newair.com.

For reference, a two-car garage will need a heater ranging from 30,000-50,000 BTUs to reach a consistent, comfortable temperature.

Recent findings suggest that whether you attempt the electrical work or hire it out, Shapiro has two more recommendations. First, don’t install the heater so that a power cord leading to a machine or tool could be draped directly in front of it. The heat can damage the cord.

In a recent development, second, consider installing a CO alarm in the garage. A CO alarm can make the garage a safer place to work, especially if you’re heating it with gas, and it can also protect the occupants of the house.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images).

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

In a recent development, vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night.".

It has been revealed that trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over.".

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”.

According to recent reports, “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!".

In a recent development, the situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Sources indicate that trump, Vance and other administration officials have remarked in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

It has been revealed that trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "promptly.".

Sources indicate that “Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers stated in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”.

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Recent findings suggest that asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he noted: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”.
