  • According to recent reports, instead, consider adding a wood stove—an appliance that provides a country aesthetic and serves as a primary or secondary heat source.
  • Sources indicate that more than 2 million of the roughly 12.5 million wood stoves in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The crackle of a fire on a cold winter night can add charm to any home. However, fireplaces aren’t particularly efficient heat sources, especially in chilly temperatures. And electric fireplaces, space heaters, and other supplementary heat sources can leave you in the dark (and out in the cold) during a power outage.

According to recent reports, instead, consider adding a wood stove—an appliance that provides a country aesthetic and serves as a primary or secondary heat source. Modern wood stoves can be safe, affordable, and efficient if you clean and maintain them regularly.

Sources indicate that more than 2 million of the roughly 12.5 million wood stoves in the U.S. are older, uncertified models that put out far more particulate pollution than newer ones, according to the EPA, and some states prohibit or restrict these wood-burning devices. All of the wood stoves recommended here are EPA-certified, and they still crank out enough BTUs to make your home or cabin cozy.

Industry observers note that before you buy, think carefully about where you’ll install your stove. You’ll need proper clearance from combustible materials in walls and floors, and the stove’s weight has to work for your house.

Recent findings suggest that the Expert (Alex Rennie): I'm a freelance writer who specializes in the Home Improvement, DIY, and Tool space. As a former residential and commercial carpenter, I use my hands-on experience to write practical buying guides, how-to articles, and product reviews. Based in Los Angeles, I spend my free time exploring the beaches and mountains with my fiancé and our dog Louie.

According to recent reports, to choose my wood stove recommendations, I selected non-catalytic models that are affordable while still meeting EPA emissions standards. Among the wood stoves that made the cut, you’ll find a wide variety to meet your space limitations and style preferences while maintaining efficient BTU output.

Industry observers note that one of the best things about having a huge fire in the middle of your home is that it lets you make the most of those rustic vibes. Many of the stoves I picked have a cooktop (very convenient) or a large window, so you can put your feet up and enjoy watching the flames. I also relied on prior research conducted by writer Alex Rennie, who also contributed to this article.

This pedestal stove from Ashley Hearth hits the sweet spot between size, heat output, and price. Its 2,500-square-foot heating range fits the average home with room to spare, and the brick-lined, 2.7-cubic-foot firebox accepts logs up to 21 inches long. That means fewer trips to the woodpile on cold nights.

Industry observers note that one of the best features is the cast iron door with air-washed ceramic glass, which helps keep soot off the window so you can enjoy the view of the fire. A non-catalytic secondary burn extracts more heat from every load and keeps emissions within EPA standards. It’s mobile-home approved when paired with the optional fresh air kit. The stove runs fine without electricity, but an optional blower will help push warm air into the rest of your house.

If you don’t need to heat your entire home, this compact Ashley Hearth model delivers plenty of warmth for the money. Its 68,000 BTU output covers up to 1,200 square feet. That makes it a smart fit for a cabin or an open living area, or as a supplemental heat source that takes some pressure off your furnace.

Sources indicate that it shares many features with our Best Overall pick, including a firebrick-lined firebox and a non-catalytic secondary burn that keeps emissions within EPA standards. It also has a heavy cast iron door with air-washed ceramic glass. It ships with both legs and a pedestal, so you can choose the look that suits your space. At 258 pounds, it’s relatively easy to move into place, and it’s mobile-home approved with the optional fresh air kit. The trade-off is a smaller 1.3-cubic-foot firebox, so you’ll load logs more often than with a larger stove.

According to recent reports, if watching the fire matters more to you than heating every corner of the house, this Superior stove is built around the view. A large rectangular ceramic-glass door gives you a wide view of the flames, and the built-in air-wash system sweeps air across the glass to keep soot off.

According to recent reports, the high-density firebrick holds heat longer for a more efficient burn. It puts out just 2.1 grams of particulate per hour, well under EPA limits. It fits logs up to 18 inches long, and one control handles the airflow. A black pedestal base comes standard, and an optional variable-speed blower can push warm air into nearby rooms.

The trade-off is a heating range of up to 1,400 square feet, so it’s best suited to a living room, a cabin, or a smaller home.

The WoodPro 300 is the largest model in the WoodPro line, built for anyone heating a large open floor plan, a farmhouse, or a drafty workshop. Its 2.26-cubic-foot firebox takes 18-inch logs and can burn for up to 12 hours on a single load, so you won’t have to refill it every couple of hours.

Recent findings suggest that the stove is made of heavy-gauge steel with a cast-iron door. The Smart Air Control uses two levers, so the lighting procedure is simple: get the fire going, set the air, and leave it alone. It meets EPA 2020 standards at 1.6 grams of smoke per hour with 74.2 percent efficiency, and it’s approved for mobile homes with the outside air kit. Its peak output of 61,700 BTU is modest for a stove rated for 3,000 square feet, so treat that number as a best case in a well-insulated home, not something to count on in a cold climate.

This rustic model from Ashley Hearth—under the US Stove Organization umbrella—the US1269E, is a natural fit for log cabin homes that want a rugged addition to their living space, or for anyone looking to add woodsy charm to their home.

My favorite feature is the oversized safety handle, which is comfortable to grab when opening or closing the door and stays cool to the touch, even when the stove is in operation.

Tested and certified to U.L.1482 by Warnock Hersey International, this stove’s 900-square-foot heating range isn’t the largest of my selections, but it's still impressive for its size. The integrated cooking surface on top is also a valuable feature.

If you’re looking for a pint-sized stove for a small space, including a mobile home, US Stove's Tiny Wood Stove may provide the perfect fit. The slim profile doesn’t mean it’s short on efficiency or on meeting emissions standards, and it still qualifies for the 30-percent Biomass federal tax credit.

A compact design, however, comes with a few caveats, including a rather small log size and a relatively low BTU output. Still, the US Stove Tiny Stove is a great trade-off for a single-room cabin or a more compact space in your home.

Recent findings suggest that wood stoves come in all shapes, sizes, and designs. Choose one that suits your space in terms of style and efficiency. Here’s how to decide what you need in a wood stove and what you don't.

According to recent reports, there are two types of modern wood stoves: catalytic and non-catalytic. Both reduce air pollution by reburning exhaust to limit emissions, but catalytic stoves use a different process that is slightly more efficient at this second burn. Non-catalytic stoves are popular because they’re less expensive and slightly more efficient at producing heat.

Because the cost of a wood stove with a catalytic converter is presently prohibitive for the average homeowner, the wood stove models we’ve recommended below are all non-catalytic.

More Hot Stuff: Smokeless Fire Pits • Fire Pit Tables • Portable Fire Pits • Heated Blankets.

The size of your wood stove matters not just for the space it can heat, but also for safety. Before you install a wood stove, check your state requirements for clearance. Federal guidelines stipulate that the stove should be installed at least 3 feet from any combustibles in the wall, ceiling, or floors.

If you have children, also consider how much clearance you might need around the stove for a child safety gate and where you strategy to stack and store firewood.

British Thermal Units (BTUs) might sound fancy, but it's just a measurement of how much heat is being generated. This differs from the heating area of a wood stove because it refers to the energy the stove produces in an hour. A rule of thumb: You need 20 BTUs for every foot of space you want to heat. Use this online BTU calculator to dial in exactly how many thermal units your home needs.

In a recent development, decide whether you’re using your wood stove as a main heating source or for supplemental heat in the winter. In general, a small wood stove can heat about 500 square feet, while a medium wood stove warms up to 1,000 square feet. A large model will heat a room of 1,500 square feet or more.

More isn’t always better. To keep costs in check and your wood stove efficient, consider if you really need to heat every space in your home or just the living areas your family frequents.

Modern wood stoves are lighter than ever, but many large models can still tip the scales at several hundred pounds. Depending on the stove's weight, you may not be able to install it in a mobile home or in certain structurally vulnerable spots in your house. Instead, look for a wood stove approved for mobile homes by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).

If your goal is an outdoor wood stove portable enough for camping or backpacking, choose a lightweight model with components that collapse into a compact package.

Industry observers note that the size of the logs and the kind of wood you put into your wood stove is about more than convenience or cost. It can also affect burn time and efficiency, which is especially key if you’re using your wood stove as a main heating source.

Generally, most wood stoves fit logs about 16 inches long and 3 inches in diameter. As you can imagine, wood stoves designed for smaller logs may leave you rolling up your sleeves and grabbing the axe more often than you might like.

Since 2020, nearly all fresh wood stoves sold in the United States must be certified by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to meet its 2020 emissions standards, which limit fine particle pollution to 2.0 grams per hour (2.5 g/h when tested with cordwood). All of the wood stoves we’ve recommended below meet this standard, and you can look up any model in the EPA’s database of certified wood-burning heaters.

Recent findings suggest that A wood stove’s effectiveness in converting wood into heat is expressed as a percentage of combustion efficiency. Efficiency matters because it directly translates into how much wood you’ll burn to keep your home warm. Most modern EPA-certified stoves fall between 70 and 80 percent efficiency, and every few points add up over a full heating season in fewer logs split, stacked, and hauled inside.

It has been revealed that from insulating the chimney to adhering to proper stovepipe clearance, to wall shields and floor pads, there’s quite a bit to do when you install a wood stove, and much of it is mandated by building codes and state or federal laws. To protect your safety, it's critical that you don't miss a step, which is why I recommend leaving the installation of the wood stove to a professional.

Clean your wood stove (and chimney) thoroughly and often to avoid creosote buildup, a highly flammable byproduct of burning wood.

Sources indicate that while cleaning your chimney, tidying up your wood stove is pretty straightforward. When the stove is cool, lay down a cloth or newspaper, then empty the ashtray and any ashes from the firebox into an ash bucket. Then wait at least 24 to 48 hours before you dump the ash bucket so any slightly warm embers don’t catch fire.

You can wipe down the interior with a soft, wet cloth and use a chimney brush to scrub out the stovepipe and loosen any residue. If the exterior has rust, you can use a wire brush or sandpaper to remove it.

Yes, you can leave a wood stove unattended for a few hours or overnight, but with some caveats. You should tamp down or mostly close some vents to ensure the fire stays under control. Also, shut and lock the door, and clear any objects from around the stove.

Just be aware that if you initiative to leave the fire unattended and it goes out overnight, you’ll have to restart it, which is harder than simply feeding a live fire.

In a recent development, most upcoming wood stoves you can buy in the U.S. will be EPA-certified, but you should still check the packaging to verify.

EPA certification means the wood stove has been independently tested to meet a particulate emissions limit of no more than 4.5 grams per hour. If you have an old model that is not EPA-certified, check whether your state has a program that provides tax deductions for replacing your wood stove.

Three Routes to VPP Revenue for Installers, EPCs, and Developers Utility programs, wholesale markets, and bilateral contracts each come with different eligibility rules, payment structures, and commercial responsibilities.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in June 2026, Google and Voltus announced a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM.
  • Recent findings suggest that the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs.
  • In a recent development, utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Intersolar & Energy Storage North America.

According to recent reports, in June 2026, Google and Voltus announced a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM. Under Voltus’s Bring Your Own Capacity model, Google funds procurement while Voltus aggregates qualifying distributed energy resources (DERs) and compensates participating customers.1.

Recent findings suggest that the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs. Across the U.S., utility programs, wholesale electricity markets, and bilateral contracts each have their own eligibility requirements, payment structures and commercial responsibilities.

Utility programs and procurement.

In a recent development, utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need. Payments may be tied to enrollment, committed capacity, measured performance or a combination of these factors. Massachusetts, for example, offers residential battery customers $275 per kW of average summer performance through ConnectedSolutions2.

Beyond customer incentive programs, utilities also procure distributed flexibility through contracts to address local grid constraints or broader capacity needs. Unlike standardized incentives, these arrangements can establish specific delivery requirements and compensation terms, creating opportunities for developers and service providers to assemble and manage DER portfolios. During a July 2026 heat event, Green Mountain Power dispatched 90 MW of stored energy capacity, helping customers avoid an estimated $6 million in peak-related costs during one peak hour3.

Aggregated DERs can earn revenue from energy, capacity, and ancillary services in wholesale electricity markets, subject to regional market rules and resource qualification. Unlike utility-specific programs, wholesale markets can provide access to broader regional revenue opportunities and multiple grid services. For developers and installers, participation typically occurs through an aggregator or other qualified market participant rather than through direct market registration.

Recent findings suggest that while Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order 2222 established a broader framework for DER participation, uneven implementation across regional markets continues to constrain commercial opportunities for aggregated resources. Market access does not automatically translate into revenue, as individual resources must still meet qualification requirements and comply with market-specific rules. Fresh York Independent System Operator (NYISO), for example, requires DER aggregations to meet minimum capacity and real-time telemetry requirements, which can increase participation costs and limit the economic viability of smaller resources.

Wholesale participation can also expose VPP portfolios to fluctuating market prices, performance obligations and restrictions on receiving compensation for overlapping services. In Texas, ERCOT’s Aggregate Distributed Energy Resource (ADER) pilot allows aggregated DERs to participate in wholesale energy and ancillary services markets, subject to qualification, telemetry, and dispatch requirements.

Bilateral contracts and emerging buyers.

In a recent development, bilateral contracts allow utilities and large electricity consumers to procure distributed flexibility directly from aggregators and service providers. Growing interest from data center operators and other large energy buyers is expanding the potential market for VPP capacity beyond traditional utility programs. Unlike standardized programs, bilateral agreements can be tailored to a buyer’s specific needs, with negotiated terms for capacity, delivery periods, compensation, and performance obligations.

The appropriate route depends on existing customer relationships, market access, and the responsibilities each partner assumes. Developers and EPCs working on commercial storage projects may find opportunities through utility procurement or capacity contracts, while residential installers with established battery customer bases may be well positioned to incorporate VPP enrollment into utility programs. Wholesale markets can expand revenue opportunities through aggregation partners, and bilateral contracts can create opportunities to develop resources around specific buyer needs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • When astronomers first spotted the supernova now designated SN 2026ahvu, it was just one of the dozens detected every day.
  • “I think almost everyone in the world is trying to trigger a telescope and look at this,” states astrophysicist Sumit Sarbadhicary of Johns Hopkins University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

When astronomers first spotted the supernova now designated SN 2026ahvu, it was just one of the dozens detected every day. But scientists soon realized this one was something very special, and they’ve been hustling to study it ever since.

“I think almost everyone in the world is trying to trigger a telescope and look at this,” states astrophysicist Sumit Sarbadhicary of Johns Hopkins University.

Soon after scientists spotted the explosion on November 2, they determined it hadn’t yet peaked in brightness, giving scientists an early glimpse at the event. Even more thrilling, within a day of the explosion’s discovery, astronomers had classified it as a type Ia supernova. These particular outbursts are rare, but they’re astronomical superstars: Scientists use their trademark explosion pattern as a “standard candle” to measure distance into the universe — most notably to discover that the universe’s expansion is accelerating. And to round out a trifecta of reasons to be excited, these blasts rarely occur so close to Earth.

Astronomers know type 1a supernovas occur upon the reignition and resulting self-destruction of a white dwarf star, the small cool remnants of a star like the sun that’s too small to become a superdense neutron star or black hole at its demise. Scientists also know that powering back on requires reaching about 1.44 times the mass of the sun, which can occur only if something is giving the white dwarf extra mass.

But scientists aren’t sure what that something is — whether these supernovas are triggered by a second white dwarf or some sort of star that’s still burning. Usually, these explosions occur so far away that astronomers can’t get a good look at where they come from. But SN 2026ahvu is perhaps 50 million light-years or less away from Earth.

“They happen so rarely at this distance that it could hopefully help us figure out why this white dwarf exploded in the first place,” says astronomer Yvette Cendes of the University of Oregon in Eugene, who has been arranging for radio telescopes to observe the outburst.

Sarbadhicary and colleagues have already submitted preliminary findings November 6 at arXiv.org suggesting that the former white dwarf was less than 100 million years old. That’s remarkably young compared with other supernovas of this type, and may help scientists finetune their understanding of these outbursts.

“These explosions have been enduring mysteries for us for decades, and whenever something happens this close, it’s just really exciting,” Sarbadhicary indicates.

In a recent development, former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once stated he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

In a recent development, the Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

Recent findings suggest that “Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, stated in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”.

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

According to recent reports, golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

Sources indicate that “I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Industry observers note that dunlap initially rolled out his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

#145932. Vortex Crossfire vs. Leupold BX-3: Compact, Lightweight, Affordable Options That Offer More Than What Most Need

Vortex Crossfire vs. Leupold BX-3: Compact, Lightweight, Affordable Options That Offer More Than What Most Need

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • It has been revealed that whether you’re spotting deer while on a hunt or identifying backyard birds, a trusty pair of 10x42 binoculars is a must-have for the outdoors.
  • Sources indicate that most people want a pair of binoculars that is decent, but not so exceptional that they have to spend thousands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that whether you’re spotting deer while on a hunt or identifying backyard birds, a trusty pair of 10x42 binoculars is a must-have for the outdoors. The 10x magnification isn’t too tight for closer quarters—think birdwatching—but gives you enough reach to spot animals 1,000 yards away, and it’s even sufficient for casual stargazing. The 42 mm objective lens (the one farther from your eyes) is wide enough to let in lots of light while keeping the field of vision natural.

Sources indicate that most people want a pair of binoculars that is decent, but not so exceptional that they have to spend thousands. I recommend the $150 to $300 range to get high-quality glass with coatings and enough performance that you won’t ever feel the need to upgrade.

In a recent development, both the Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42 ($300) and the Leupold BX-3 ($230) fall right in this entry-level sweet spot. We tested both for our Best Binoculars buying guide and selected the Leupold BX-3 10x42 as our favorite binocular overall, but the Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42 performed very well, considering the price (often available for much less than retail, as it’s an older model than the Leupold, which debuted this year). As such, we compared the two head-to-head to identify meaningful differences. Here’s what we found.

Vortex Crossfire vs. Leupold BX-3.

Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42 Binoculars.

I tested the Crossfire and BX-3 both handheld and tripod-mounted side-by-side in a range of conditions including sunset low-light environments, dense forest, long-distance expanses in the mountains, and several specialized setups designed to test things such as chromatic aberration, color fidelity, and image sharpness.

Truly objective stats about binocular performance can be hard to come by, so the somewhat arbitrary “tiers” of binoculars defined by price and place in a firm’s lineup can serve as useful shorthand for how impressive the optical quality is.

Leupold’s BX-3 Alpine HD 10x42 binos are on the lower “budget” end of the manufacturer's numbered BX lineup that goes all the way up to the $3,999 BX-6 Range HD RangeFinder 10x42 binoculars. Still, I would argue that this tier of binocular at 10x42 offers you most of the performance of the high-end models. The higher you go in price, in my experience, the smaller the gains in clarity and performance.

In a recent development, vortex has many different lines, each one representing small jumps in features and optical quality. The Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42 sits between its Triumph and Viper lines—the Triumph is our Best Budget and the Viper is Best for Hunting. The Crossfire HD 10x42 is entry-level in terms of price but is likely to be all the binoculars most people need, and still feels like a significant cost if binoculars are a nice-to-have item for you.

In terms of size and specs, the Leupold BX-3 10x42 is likely most comparable to the Vortex Viper HD 10x42, but at $749 MSRP doesn’t feel like an apples-to-apples comparison. The Viper HDs are great binoculars, especially for hunters who demand the dawn and dusk performance, but their price is more than double that of the BX-3 Alpine HD.

Note that both brands’ binos are usually available at retailers for much less than the MSRP on the official sites. At the time of this writing, the $230 Crossfire can be had in several places for $150 while the $299 BX-3 binos are consistently $199 at Scheel’s and Cabela’s, making the two models fairly close on real-world price.

Sources indicate that both brands market to the hunting community and it demonstrates in these fairly similar designs. The roof prism design on both the BX-3 and Crossfire is near-standard in this type of binocular and it helps keep the size and weight down compared to bulkier designs used in the cheapest binos.

Recent findings suggest that the Crossfire binos have a slightly flared look as you move from the eyepieces to the exit lenses while the Leupold are straighter, but the overall form factor is very similar. The Vortex Crossfire is slightly longer at 6 inches compared to the 5.7-inch Leupold BX-3.

Practically, these are both relatively compact, lightweight binos that will fit in most any aftermarket chest harness and won’t cause neck strain as promptly as bigger glass. The Crossfire is 0.4 ounces heavier than the BX—not really a meaningful difference in practice.

Recent findings suggest that both have hard plastic eyecups by default, which are more durable than the floppy rubber ones that often come on the cheapest binos. Leupold’s BX-3, however, comes with two other swappable eyecup options. During sunrise and sunset glassing, when low-angle sunlight constantly sneaks into your peripheral vision and nukes contrast, the alternate eyecups block the intrusions, making a legitimately noticeable difference.

This is the most crucial aspect of binoculars and also the hardest to objectively compare. Testing binoculars in person is always a smart idea if possible, as a few minutes scanning store shelves under artificial light isn't a great real-world test.

According to recent reports, both models provide decent center-image sharpness, especially considering their low cost. Moving closer to the edge of the image, clarity degrades in any binocular. The Leupold BX-3 binos have a slightly larger center area of sharpness than the Crossfire, perhaps 80 percent versus 70 percent.

It has been revealed that A small but noticeable difference that subtly adds to the comfort of using them and gives Leupold an edge. In real-world use spotting animals such as bighorn sheep at long distances, I didn’t even notice. Like many marginal improvements you get with better binos, the sharper image just adds subtly to the overall picture clarity. For hunters, it’s unlikely to be the difference between success and failure, but it may make long sessions a touch easier and more enjoyable.

Sources indicate that I expected much more noticeable color fringing with the Crossfire HD, but it wasn’t pronounced in either pair. This defect in imagery in binocular views and photography occurs when light gets distorted and unnatural colors appear, usually around the edges of objects such as dark hair on an animal appearing blue or purple.

Sources indicate that both the Crossfire and BX-3 have HD in the name, which most likely refers to the glass elements and coating that help reduce glare, fringing, and generally produce a sharper image. For the most part, I noticed few differences in object sharpness and color. Both binos produce refreshingly neutral, natural colors in a range of light conditions.

Sources indicate that glare was less pronounced in the Leupold BX-3 Alpine HD than the Vortex Crossfire HD. Neither was able to eliminate glare entirely in challenging conditions such as pointing roughly 20 degrees off from the sun near sunset. But the portion of the view obscured by glare was smaller in the BX-3. It was also less hazy and diffuse, which left the portion of the view not obscured by glare clearer. This is, again, not a massive difference but adds incrementally to a slightly better optical quality overall for the BX-3.

Dusk, dawn, and dark forests are an extreme that can expose cheaper binoculars. For hunters, the crepuscular hours are when animals are usually most active—and when they’re hardest to pick out through your optics. Birdwatchers and casual customers will be less affected if a bino struggles to gather dwindling light, but performance in these conditions is a reasonable indicator of overall optical quality.

Sources indicate that the Leupold BX-3 was noticeably better in the worst, last-minute-of-the-day conditions, but the differences were only pronounced at the extremes. The brighter image wasn’t noticeable until well into the “blue hour” that comes before sunrise and after sunset. This makes using brighter optics much easier for hunters desperately scanning dwindling light but might not sway more casual users. The brightness of the two pairs was mostly indistinguishable in midday sun.

According to recent reports, these are fairly closely matched binoculars, though the Leupold was the better pair whenever there was an edge to be had. The most meaningful separators were low-light brightness and center-image sharpness.

I didn’t find this surprising as the Leupold BX-3 Alpine HD costs more, and the Vortex Crossfire HD is more of an entry-level option that sits maybe one level below the BX-3 in the loose optical hierarchy of grades of binoculars. Rather than an apples-to-oranges comparison, testing these side-by-side served as a reminder of how subtle the improvements are between tiers and price jumps in the binocular world.

In a recent development, while dedicated hunters and birders might be willing to pay $50 to $100 more for the jump in quality to the BX-3, the affordability of the Crossfire HD will appeal to those who don’t need 10 percent better. Either pair presents a good value in their respective categories, but you’ll have to decide which you value more—a lower price or better performance in challenging conditions.

At the Races: Regional realignment

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.
  • In a recent development, last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout.
  • One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

In a recent development, last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, Fresh England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.).

One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged New England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”.

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

In a recent development, three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”.

In a recent development, #MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

According to recent reports, redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a newly introduced congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a upcoming congressional map.

It has been revealed that california contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Industry observers note that guv update: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

It has been revealed that #TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Senator Morrison? Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have launched a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is Upcoming Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Industry observers note that congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, fresh members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”.

Ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The Upcoming York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Sources indicate that here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

How Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

According to recent reports, was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”.

Song of the cycle: The New York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The Fresh York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

Recent findings suggest that as of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

Recent findings suggest that if those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

#145927. The 8 Best Smokers to Cook Low and Slow

📅 30 Aug 2019 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3451 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popularmechanics ↗ Open Full Page

The 8 Best Smokers to Cook Low and Slow

📅 30 Aug 2019 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3451 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that the best smokers help you achieve the sweet and savory flavor combinations that make smoked meat so tasty.
  • There isn’t just one type of smoker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that the best smokers help you achieve the sweet and savory flavor combinations that make smoked meat so tasty. Whether pulled pork, brisket, ribs, or chicken is on the menu, this type of specialized home grill brings a new dimension to your backyard barbecues all year long.

There isn’t just one type of smoker. Purists prefer the iconic offset or “barrel” smoker, which reflects an array of regional barbecue traditions found in Texas, Memphis, Kansas City, and the Carolinas. In the last decade or so, increased interest in the art of barbecue has led to an expanded range of more beginner-friendly alternatives, including hardwood charcoal smokers and low-maintenance wood pellet smokers.

Some models have made the cooking process even easier with WiFi-enabled smart features for monitoring and adjusting internal temperature via an app on your phone. That way, you don’t have to stand by for hours as you cook.

Sources indicate that if you’re in the market for a new smoker, we have one for every setup and skill level. Continue reading for our choices of the best smokers and tips on what to consider before you buy.

We’ve tested dozens of grills and smokers of all different shapes and sizes over the years. Tony Carrick, coauthor of this article, presently uses a Masterbuilt charcoal-fed gravity smoker and a Weber Smokey Joe at home. David Dritsas is a reviews editor at Popular Mechanics and is an amateur cook who has tested a variety of grills. Both drew on their combined experience with smokers, along with external research, to inform our recommendations.

Industry observers note that we supplemented our own experience and criteria for smokers with extensive research into the various types that are available. We compared specifications of dozens of smokers and consulted user reviews to find trends or qualities that stand out (both positively and negatively) and might impact your ultimate choice. Our final recommendations span a range of designs and price points, and each offers solid performance, durable build quality, and great value.

One of the first things you notice about the Pit Boss Navigator 1600M is how well-constructed it is. The metal frame is sturdy, the hardware is strong, and the main section is well-insulated, including a heavy hood that is lined all the way around the edges by a fireproof, padded seal that keeps the heat in. (The Navigator performed very well in that regard.).

Industry observers note that it has a large hopper that holds up to 30 pounds of pellets, and the controls are easy to understand. There’s WiFi on board, and we experienced a one-time issue where the app disconnected and would not reconnect, but it otherwise worked well, and navigation was intuitive. The Navigator also has two wired thermometer probes, for which you can set temperature alerts, so you know when your meats are ready.

For our main cooking test, we smoked a flat iron steak, as well as a mix of garlic-marinated zucchini, onions, and red peppers (that was enclosed in aluminum foil, open at the top). We were impressed with how swiftly the grill heated up and how efficiently it maintained the temperature (even as we grilled in cold weather).

The only feature we did not find exceptional was the flame broil setting, which allows you to expose food to the flames of the burner cup directly. While it technically works, the cooking area of this feature is only roughly 3 inches in diameter, so it’s not very effective for large pieces of meat or more than one burger. But that complaint is a minor one.

Full Pit Boss Navigator 1600M Review.

You don’t have to spend a lot of money to get proficient at smoking food, and Oklahoma Joe’s Laredo Deluxe proves that point. It’s a very basic charcoal barrel-shaped model that requires you to stay near and mind the coals to maintain the temperature, but it offers a few nice extra features to help you do it.

It has been revealed that the biggest is the three-position charcoal tray. Set it high to sear meat while grilling or set it low to help keep temperatures down around 250 degrees Fahrenheit when smoking low and slow. Of course, airflow is integral to smoking, and there are three control options here, including a side vent, a chimney, and a large front door that you can also open to gain access to the coals for adjustment without having to remove the cooking grates. We used it several times to spread out the charcoal when things were getting a bit too hot.

There’s also a built-in thermometer that’s easy to read, even from a short distance, two side tables, and a lower shelf. All mentioned and done, even if you don’t use it as a smoker, we think this makes for a fantastic charcoal grill with plenty of cooking area (940 square inches) to make a ton of burgers for your next barbecue party.

The Laredo Deluxe is not as solidly constructed as some of the other selections on our list, but that’s to be expected for a grill that’s usually on sale for under $300. We smoked a delicious brisket with ease during our tests, and we’d happily do so again.

Full Oklahoma Joe’s Laredo Deluxe Grill and Smoker Review.

Masterbuilt’s Gravity Series 800 gives you unique flavor from hardwood charcoal smoke in your barbecue without dealing with all the fuss of micromanaging your smoker. It pairs a large gravity-fed hopper for hardwood charcoal with a digital thermostat that controls the internal temperature. The hopper keeps your cooking fire fed, while an internal fan system regulates temperature to maintain consistency. Just load it up, light it, and let it cook for hours with minimal maintenance.

Industry observers note that as with our top pick, the Gravity Series 800 features wireless-enabled smart controls, which allow you to monitor the temperature from your phone. It also includes a digital meat probe.

Sources indicate that with 800 square inches of cooking surface, you’re getting a lot of space here. There’s plenty of room for ribs, whole chickens, and pork butts. But at nearly five feet wide, the Masterbuilt 800 is a big boy—possibly too big for some decks and patios. That remarked, it also functions as a standard charcoal grill and a flat-top griddle, so you could ditch your standard grill to make space for it.

Industry observers note that this Woodridge Pro is a midrange model in Traeger’s line of pellet smokers, featuring some of the technology found in its higher-end models but at a lower price. When we unboxed the grill, we were impressed by how easy it was to put together, despite the large number of loose parts. Traeger’s assembly guide was one of the best we’ve seen, with clear directions and marked boxes with icons that corresponded to the instructions.

According to recent reports, some construction elements, such as light plastic wheels and thin grill grates, seemed lacking, and there’s no seal around the interior of the hood (which helps with heat retention). Once together, however, this grill is sturdy and not at all difficult to move around. We really appreciate that the top of the pellet hopper serves as an extra shelf, which is handy and something you don’t always get with other grills. There’s also a special pellet sensor that lets you know if pellets are running low.

The Woodridge Pro is extremely straightforward to operate. The rather retro display with large block numbers is readable from a distance, and basic temperature control is quick to adjust and set with a large push-button dial. You can also set a timer, check probe temperature, and with the press of a button, add extra smoky flavor for slow cooks under 225 degrees Fahrenheit. One thing we really liked was a motion graphic that reveals whether the grill is heating up or lowering the temperature. During our tests, it was helpful to have that feature as a reminder as we multitasked. Wireless control is available with WiFi and Bluetooth, and the app, named WiFire, is easy to use.

The food we made turned out delicious, whether slow-cooked for a deeper smoky flavor or grilled at a higher temperature for just a hint. We used both the included wired probe to monitor temperature, as well as a Meater thermometer, and found some slight discrepancies between the grill’s temperature setting and the ambient temperature on the Meater. We found ourselves pushing the temperature up a few degrees to get it where we wanted it to be. This didn’t mar the experience too greatly, however. The Woodridge Pro is a reliable pellet grill that’s fun to use and a worthy addition to any back patio.

Full Traeger Woodridge Pro Review.

It has been revealed that in many ways, the 18-Inch Smokey Mountain from Weber is a standard water smoker (a 14-inch model is also available). Like similar models, it has a bottom rack and retaining ring for the charcoal, a large bowl for water, and two racks for smoking food. But it stands out because it’s made from heavier porcelain-enameled steel, which helps retain heat and maintain a consistent temperature, as well as a heat shield on the bottom to protect your deck or lawn. It also comes with a cover.

It has been revealed that when we first fired it up to season the smoker, we took the opportunity to get familiar with how to use the three air vents around the bottom, as well as the top vent, to help hold a desired temperature. To help you gauge this, there’s a thermometer in the lid that indicates a highlighted smoking zone from 200 to 275 degrees Fahrenheit, and we found it was relatively easy to keep it in that range.

It has been revealed that we put this to the real-world test when smoking some beef jerky. To do this, we wanted to keep the temperature on the lower side at around 200 degrees Fahrenheit. This proved a little challenging; the temperature kept creeping up, so we watched it closely and adjusted the vents as needed. In the end, the jerky smoked a bit faster than we intended. In hindsight, we used a little too much charcoal, which generated more heat than we needed. While this was our mistake, it shows just how well this smoker can retain heat.

When smoking a smaller-sized brisket, we more successfully managed the temperature and were able to hold close to 225 degrees Fahrenheit for the 5 hours it took to smoke it. One thing we really appreciated during longer smoking sessions was the large door, which made it easy to add fuel and wood chips. The Smokey Mountain is a basic smoker that will require a little experience to use effectively, but will ultimately be worth the time and produce great results. — tested by Bradley Ford.

It has been revealed that though they are frowned upon by traditionalists, electric smokers like this one from East Oak are the quickest way for newly introduced barbecuers to enter the world of smoking. Its digital controls make it easy to maintain specific temperatures, and the combination of a side wood chip loader and glass door means you can check on your cook without opening the door, which could impact your cooking temperature.

The 725-square-inch cooking surface gives you plenty of room to experiment with various types of food in a single session, but the smoker itself is quite slim, measuring nearly 19 inches wide and 18 inches deep, so it won’t take up a lot of space on your deck or patio. Bottom line: This is a straightforward and, above all, convenient way to try smoking barbecue at home.

If a grill could be a pop-culture icon, the Big Green Egg is it. The brand has a whole group of fans—known as Eggheads—who gather at grilling events called EGGfests held all across the country. And it’s not just home enthusiasts. According to the tech giant, nearly 1,800 restaurants use this extremely popular kamado grill. Its excellent heat retention and temperature range, enabled by its shape and porcelain-coated ceramic enclosures, make them an instant upgrade over your average gas or charcoal grill.

That thick ceramic body is also very effective at retaining heat, making it very effective for cooking low and slow. Just add some smoking wood, and you can smoke a brisket overnight. This grill can get as hot as 750 degrees Fahrenheit when you’re grilling, but smokers will want to maintain a stable 225 to 300 degrees using the air vents at the top and the bottom of the egg. And it’s large enough to feed a crowd—we’re talking about smoking a 20-pound turkey for Thanksgiving.

This small electric smoker from GE lets you take your smoking indoors. It uses two heat sources—one to cook food and the other to burn pellets—along with a filtration device to prevent the smoke from filling your kitchen. Its modest 293 square inches of cooking surface is enough to smoke three half racks of ribs or a small pork butt.

It has been revealed that there’s a bevy of controls for setting smoke levels and adjusting temperatures. There are also preset food settings, including brisket, ribs, pork butt, and chicken wings. Built-in probes and WiFi connectivity let you monitor meat temperatures remotely, and this smoker is compatible with voice controls via Amazon Alexa and Google Home.

Full GE Indoor Electric Smoker Review.

Traditional offset or “barrel” smokers feature two parts: A large main cooking chamber for your food and a smaller cook box for the fuel. The wood or charcoal burns, heating the main chamber and filling it with smoke, which slowly cooks the meat with indirect heat and infuses it with smoky flavor. Offset smokers, like the Royal Gourmet model we recommend as our Best Value pick, are beloved by barbecue aficionados, but are also the most challenging to use. Learning how to control the temperature in an offset smoker takes practice.

Vertical or “cabinet” smokers have a tall, closet-like design with a single door on the front and three to five racks for food inside. The heat source sits in the base, allowing the heat and smoke to waft upward and fill the space. Going high instead of wide makes a vertical smoker more compact, so it’s a good option if you don’t have much room on your patio. That said, the narrow profile may limit your ability to cook large pieces of meat, such as a full rack of ribs.

Like vertical smokers, the pill-shaped bullet smoker has a fuel area at the bottom with the main cooking chamber above. Vents on the bottom and top of the smoker allow you to control the temperature inside the chamber, and a water pan sits just below the cook area to keep food moist. Bullet smokers are compact, however, and some models are stacked so tightly that you may have trouble accessing the food on the middle racks mid-cook.

It has been revealed that most pellet smokers, including the Traeger Ironwood 885, look more like a grill than a smoker, with a wide cook box and a clamshell lid that opens up to reveal a broad cooking surface. To generate smoke and heat, an electric auger feeds small hardwood pellets from a hopper on the back or side into a fire inside the cook box. The auger automatically adds fuel to the fire based on the temperature you dial in on the smoker’s digital thermostat, so you don’t need to babysit the smoker to maintain the proper temperature. However, they require a power source and tend to be the most expensive.

Kamado grills, like the famous Substantial Green Egg, are hybrid grill-smokers. These large, acorn-shaped ceramic cook boxes can maintain low temperatures for many hours or build up scorching heat with temperatures that eclipse 800 degrees. It’s an incredibly versatile option, which has made it a gateway device for fresh barbecuers.

According to recent reports, smokers can use a variety of fuel types, including hardwood, charcoal, gas, electricity, or wood pellets. Hardwood and charcoal are the fuels of choice for smoking purists. This combination creates a lot of smoke, maximizing that flavor. Maintaining a consistent low temperature takes time to learn, though, and it makes more of a mess with leftover ash.

Industry observers note that electric and gas smokers are convenient because they require little to no maintenance, but they don’t inherently produce smoke. Instead, they rely on wood chip trays that aren’t as effective as wood, charcoal, or pellets at instilling flavor into food. However, they still can produce decent results.

Pellet smokers use compressed wood pellets that generate real smoke for instilling flavor into food, while minimizing maintenance with automatic temperature regulation. Pellet grills offer excellent heat retention and temperature control, but don’t need as much constant attention as charcoal or wood grills.

Smoking meat can take eight hours or more, depending on the cut, so you’ll probably want to cook as much as you can in one session. It’s notable to look for a smoker with an efficient interior design that has space for everything you want to cook. The average cooking surface size for a smoker is around 550 square inches, which is enough to fit five full racks of ribs, four whole chickens, or five pork butts. That remarked, I’ve seen cooking surfaces range in size from 250 square inches to more than 800.

Recent findings suggest that some modern smokers can connect to your smartphone via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, allowing you to track their internal temperature, change temperature settings, and monitor meat probes remotely through an app. They can also send you alerts if the smoker’s internal temperature rises or falls, the food reaches a target temperature, or if it’s low on fuel, allowing you to keep tabs on your smoker without having to hover over it.

What’s the best temperature for smoking meat?

It has been revealed that with a smoker, you want to keep the temperature low and cook for a long time. Depending on what you’re cooking, I’d recommend maintaining your heat between 190 and 225 degrees. In that range, you will cook your meat slowly enough to make it incredibly tender and infuse it with smoky flavor.

How long does it take to smoke meat?

Industry observers note that it depends on what you’re cooking. Smoking a rack of ribs typically takes between four and five hours, but a pork butt may need 8 to 10 hours. Brisket is well-known for needing an especially long smoke—around 12 to 18 hours.

Can I use my gas grill as a smoker?

Recent findings suggest that technically, yes. You can add a smoker box to a gas grill, which holds wood chips to generate smoke. So long as you keep the top of the grill closed, that’s a smoker. Make sure to set up the grill so that the food is not sitting directly above the heat source, and set the burners so that the grill only heats to a maximum of 225 degrees with the lid closed.

Sources indicate that that said, it’s far from ideal. It’s more difficult to maintain the consistently low temperatures needed for smoking with a gas grill than it is with a dedicated smoker. On top of that, flames from a gas grill will not impart the same distinctive taste as a proper smoker burning charcoal or hardwood. (Purists don’t even like gas as a fuel for dedicated smokers.).

Atlas Ocean Voyages is asking guests for their opinions as it explores color concepts for its fresh sailing yacht, the Atlas Adventurer.

In a social media upgrade, the company said that four liveries are currently being considered for the hull: wine red, a steel blue, a graphite gray or an emerald green, inviting guests to vote on their favorite options by commenting on posts on its Instagram and Facebook profile.

Set to enter service in late 2028 as the fourth ship in Atlas Ocean Voyages’ fleet, the 400-guest Atlas Adventurer is currently under construction at the China Merchants shipyard in Haimen, China.

In addition to being the brand’s largest, the 26,000-ton ship will be the first sailing vessel in Atlas Ocean’s fleet, which now comprises three expedition vessels.

Earlier this year, the company built a miniature of the ship to study hydrodynamics and real-world performance, conducting trials at MARIN (Maritime Research Institute Netherlands) in Wageningen, the Netherlands.

The design is also highlighted by its green features, which include a 9-megawatt battery system that will enable near-silent operations when sailing under wind power.

With an ice-class rated hull, the Adventurer will offer both traditional and expedition itineraries, expanding Atlas Ocean’s deployment to upcoming areas.

For its maiden season, the ship is scheduled to offer 15 departures across Asia, Africa and the Mediterranean, including newly introduced-to-the-company areas, such as Southeast Asia and Eastern Africa.

That’s where portable refrigerators shine, offering cooling capability that you just can’t get from a regular cooler. They’re great for long camping trips where you need to keep meat and other food at safe temperatures and come in plenty of sizes to suit hardcore camper rigs and RVs or fit in a standard sedan.

It has been revealed that portable refrigerators—often called car refrigerators—plug into your car’s 12-volt outlet, an AC outlet, or a portable power station. They’re pricier and heavier than the standard cooler, but they're more efficient at cooling. And you get to skip the expense and hassle of dealing with bags of ice. They can also be helpful around the house if your fridge breaks or there’s a power outage.

We used our expertise on coolers, power stations, and camping gear to find the best portable refrigerators. We checked camping and overlanding gear reviews and forums to find models that hold up on long treks in remote areas and are viable alternatives for people who don't want to deal with bags of ice for a cooler.

Recent findings suggest that we chose options in different capacities and across a range of prices and prioritized models that offer convenient features like USB chargers, wheels, and LED lights. If you want some extra cooling power on-the-go, consider one of the portable refrigerators for your next trek.

This portable fridge from Bodega has great build quality, convenient features for easy portability, and cools down fast. The compressor can cool the interior down to 32 degrees Fahrenheit in about 30 minutes.

It has two separate compartments to keep things organized. They can’t be individually controlled but the smaller section typically gets cooler than the larger side. It also has a user-friendly app for setting the temperature and a USB port to charge other devices. Some customers report minor differences between the temperature they see on the app versus the actual internal temperature, but say it’s only off by a couple degrees.

The portable refrigerator has sturdy handles and a built-in LED light so you can promptly find what you need in the dark. Standout features include wheels and a drain plug—two things that are standard on most larger coolers but something a lot of portable fridges lack. The lid can be opened from either side or popped off entirely for fast loading.

This portable refrigerator is a great value for efficient cooling, a low power draw, and large capacity. The 59-quart space is split into two zones for easy organizing and the unit comes with a removable wire basket.

Its tall, slender shape fits easily behind a row of seats in the car. The handles are also removable to make for easy stowing. The app lets you set and monitor temps, though you can’t do much else. Some users report the app is user-friendly but wish it had more features.

The Alpicool is a budget portable refrigerator that cools down fast to roughly zero degrees Fahrenheit and operates quietly in comparison to most other models.

According to recent reports, it has an automatic shutoff to ensure it doesn’t drain your car or portable battery and eco mode that pulls less energy. An external LCD display and control panel highlights you the interior temperature. This budget option also has an LED light inside and a drain plug.

Recent findings suggest that setup is rather easy but the included manual doesn’t show you how to convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit. The brand’s website has a detailed owner’s manual that's more helpful.

Industry observers note that thinking of Igloo might still conjure the image of the old-school Playmate cooler you had as a kid. But the ICF electric cooler is anything but that. This helps separate dry items like canned drinks from wet items like fruit and sandwiches. The ICF is also remarkably simple. Full Igloo ICF Electric Cooler Review.

The Bouge comes in a compact package that can serve as a personal cooler for a remote overnight, or extra storage on long treks. It has a single compartment that works as a fridge or freezer.

Industry observers note that set the temperature from the external control panel and monitor through the LCD thermometer. There’s no app to keep tabs on the temperature while driving but customers report it stays consistent even in hotter ambient temps. Recessed handles add to its space-saving design.

Some reviews mention the external thermometer can be off as much as seven degrees—a bit higher than most other models.

The Travoca Rigel eCooler has a number of small, but notable, features that intrigued us right away. For one, it’s somewhat modular. You can unscrew the wood paneling on the front and replace it with attachments such as a small shelf for placing drinks or snacks.

The lid is fully detachable and reversible, so you can pop the whole thing off and get a full look at everything inside. Beyond this, dual-zone cooling is powerful. Each section can work as either a fridge or freezer.

Industry observers note that and if you don’t need separate sections, the internal divider comes out, converting the entire interior to one large space at the same temperature. Travoca also sells internal baskets separately for easier organization.

Dometic is the best-known brand of portable refrigerators, with a reputation for turning out models that are durable and reliable With that comes the higher price tag, but overlanders and outdoor enthusiasts are still fans—I see this one touted most in forums as the main fridge people use while traveling on long remote treks.

It’s on the heavier side at 60 pounds when empty, but its compressor is more powerful than other models on this list—and it operates quietly.

The portable refrigerator has a sleek display and an intuitive app to set and keep tabs on the interior temperature, plus a USB port for charging for mobile devices.

According to recent reports, with a wheeled base and telescopic handles, this portable fridge from BougeRV is a well-built mix between portability and size. The interior comes with two separate sections. You can tune each to different temperatures, allowing you to have both a functional fridge and freezer at the same time.

One of the more user-friendly features the CRD2 has is an opening for a standalone battery. While sold separately, the battery allows the cooler to operate without any large power source, like a wall outlet or car, nearby. With the attached battery, the portable fridge can run for up to 20 hours with no other power source, making it an ideal way to escape to the beach or sleep overnight in the woods away from your car and still wake up to fresh produce and unspoiled milk.

In a recent development, portable refrigerators run on a compressor just like your kitchen fridge and freezer and keep food fresher a lot longer than a cooler and ice. Most reach an average minimum temperature of -4 to -7 degrees Fahrenheit to freeze and refrigerate food, though some are refrigerators only, reaching a minimum temperature of 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

Although portable refrigerators don't rely solely on insulation for cooling power, they're still well insulated enough to take some of the load off the compressor when it comes to temperature regulation.

Recent findings suggest that don’t confuse portable refrigerators with electric coolers, as that’s another product category entirely. Electric coolers rely on thermoelectric cooling, which isn’t as efficient because it's impacted by ambient temperatures. As such, they can only cool to about 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Unlike portable refrigerators, electric coolers don’t have a compressor and don’t have the power to achieve freezing temperatures.

Portable refrigerators typically draw an average of about 45 watts of power, which is less than a standard mini fridge. This won’t blow out any car fuses or drain a car battery unless the unit is kept on for days without the car running. We chose portable refrigerators that have features like eco modes and automatic shutoff so there are precautions in place to prevent it from draining a car or portable battery.

In a recent development, while portable refrigerators offer more storage than coolers because they don’t need ice, their built-in compressor makes them relatively heavy at about 30 pounds or more. Still, some are more portable than others thanks to built-in handles and wheels. They don’t have shoulder straps and aren’t meant to be carried over a far distance. Also, most don't have drain plugs like standard coolers because condensation is minimal and can easily be wiped out with a small towel.
